title: MoodMate: Six-Class Emotion Classification
text: MoodMate is a collaborative NLP and machine learning project exploring the classification of short text into six emotions: sadness, joy, love, anger, fear, and surprise. This notebook compares Logistic Regression, Multinomial Naive Bayes, and Random Forest using TF-IDF features.

title: MoodMate: Six-Class Emotion Classification
text:
Exploratory analysis
Examine the distribution of emotion labels and message lengths in the training split. Numeric labels follow the mapping defined above.

title: MoodMate: Six-Class Emotion Classification
text:
Text features
TF-IDF represents each message as a sparse vector of weighted terms. The vectorizer is fitted only on training text, then applied unchanged to validation text to avoid vocabulary leakage. English stop-word removal is retained from the original experiment; it can discard useful context, including negations, and was not separately tuned.


Training matrix shape: (16000, 14894)
Validation matrix shape: (2000, 14894)
Sample vocabulary: ['aa' 'aaaaaaand' 'aaaaand' 'aaaand' 'aac' 'aahhh' 'aaron' 'ab' 'abandon'
 'abandoned']


The original run produced a 16,000 × 14,894 training matrix and a 2,000 × 14,894 validation matrix. Each row represents a message and each column a term learned from training data.

title: MoodMate: Six-Class Emotion Classification
text:
Logistic Regression
Train a linear classifier on TF-IDF features and report per-class precision, recall, and F1-score on the validation split.


Accuracy: 0.8745
Detailed scores:
               precision    recall  f1-score   support

           0       0.88      0.94      0.91       550
           1       0.86      0.95      0.90       704
           2       0.90      0.70      0.78       178
           3       0.90      0.85      0.88       275
           4       0.87      0.74      0.80       212
           5       0.85      0.65      0.74        81

    accuracy                           0.87      2000
   macro avg       0.88      0.80      0.83      2000
weighted avg       0.88      0.87      0.87      2000



Original validation accuracy: 87.45%. The classification report shows lower recall for less frequent classes, especially surprise. Precision measures the correctness of predicted labels, recall measures coverage of true labels, and F1 balances the two.

title: MoodMate: Six-Class Emotion Classification
text:
Multinomial Naive Bayes
Compare a probabilistic text-classification baseline using the same TF-IDF features. The original model predicted no validation examples of class 5 (surprise), making its precision mathematically undefined. zero_division=0 explicitly reports this as 0; it does not fix the underlying failure. Inspect class-level recall rather than accuracy alone.


Naive Bayes Accuracy: 0.681
Naive Bayes Detailed Scores:

           0       0.66      0.93      0.77       550
           1       0.65      0.97      0.78       704
           2       1.00      0.07      0.13       178
           3       0.97      0.34      0.50       275
           4       0.95      0.28      0.44       212
           5       0.00      0.00      0.00        81

weighted avg       0.73      0.68      0.61      2000



Original validation accuracy: 68.10%. The original classification report records zero recall for surprise (class 5), and much lower recall for several minority classes. The historical warning messages are omitted because the reporting behavior is now explicit.

title: MoodMate: Six-Class Emotion Classification
text:
Interpretation and limitations
Original validation accuracies: Logistic Regression 87.45%, Naive Bayes 68.10%, and Random Forest 89.85%. Random Forest performed best on this validation split. These are historical saved outputs, not fresh verification.

The label distribution is uneven; accuracy should be considered alongside per-class precision, recall, and F1.
The companion randomForest.ipynb explores CountVectorizer and TF-IDF Random Forest variants with a separate held-out test split.

title: Stock Return Prediction & Options Pricing
text:
Tools: Python, pandas, scikit-learn, XGBoost, yfinance
Type: Independent Machine Learning & Quantitative Finance Project
Developed an end-to-end machine learning pipeline to predict whether individual stocks would outperform the S&P 500 (SPY) over the following month.
Analyzed historical price data from 20 stocks across four sectors between 2018 and 2024.



Feature Engineering: Created momentum, moving-average, and volatility indicators from historical stock prices.
Machine Learning: Trained and evaluated Logistic Regression, Ridge Classifier, and XGBoost models using a chronological train-test split.
Backtesting: Simulated a rolling stock-selection strategy that ranked stocks and selected the top five for an equally weighted portfolio.
Options Pricing: Implemented Black-Scholes and Cox-Ross-Rubinstein binomial tree models to estimate theoretical European call option prices.

title: 05 - Options Pricing
text: This notebook takes the Ridge model’s latest top stock picks and prices one-month call options on them using Black-Scholes and a Cox-Ross-Rubinstein binomial tree.

title: 05 - Options Pricing
text:
Workflow

Load daily prices and engineered monthly features.
Rebuild the long-format model dataset used by the Ridge classifier.
Train on all months before the latest feature month and score the latest month.
Pull the one-month Treasury yield from FRED as the risk-free rate.
Price 30-day call options with Black-Scholes and a binomial tree.
Compare the two prices and visualize the spread.

title: 05 - Options Pricing
text:
Recreate the Ridge top picks
The option pricing notebook uses the same six engineered factors as the modeling and backtesting notebooks. To avoid training on the target attached to the latest month, the model trains on months strictly before the latest feature date, then scores the latest month.

title: 05 - Options Pricing
section: Pull the risk-free rate from FRED
text:
Pull the risk-free rate from FRED
FRED publishes Treasury yields as percentages. This notebook uses DGS1MO, the one-month Treasury constant maturity rate, because the option maturity below is set to 30 days. If the FRED request fails, the notebook falls back to a clearly marked manual rate so the rest of the analysis can still run offline.

title: 05 - Options Pricing
text:
Pricing functions
The Black-Scholes implementation prices European calls. The binomial tree below is also configured for European calls so the comparison is apples-to-apples. For non-dividend-paying European calls, the binomial price should converge toward Black-Scholes as the number of steps rises.

title: 05 - Options Pricing
text:
Build option inputs
This baseline prices at-the-money calls using each selected stock’s latest adjusted close as both spot and strike. Volatility comes from the latest engineered feature row, where it was already annualized in Notebook 2.

title: 05 - Options Pricing
text:
Interpretation

The two prices should usually be close because both methods price the same European call under the same assumptions.
The binomial tree is discrete, so the gap versus Black-Scholes depends on the number of steps. Increasing BINOMIAL_STEPS should generally shrink the difference.
This is a theoretical premium estimate, not a tradable options quote. Real option chains include bid-ask spreads, discrete strikes, dividends, early exercise considerations, transaction costs, and implied volatility rather than historical realized volatility.
The model picks inherit the same limitations as the earlier notebooks: small sample size, survivorship bias, and no transaction costs.
